title: Reply Comments of Google LLC re the Advanced Notice of Proposed Rulemaking proposal re the Interconnection of Large Loads to the Interstate Transmission System under RM26-4.

UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                  BEFORE THE
                    FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION


                                                 )
Interconnection of Large Loads                   )                   Docket No. RM26-4-000
to the Interstate Transmission System            )
                                                 )


                            REPLY COMMENTS OF GOOGLE LLC

         Google LLC (“Google”) hereby submits these reply comments in connection with the

Advanced Notice of Proposed Rulemaking proposal (“DOE ANOPR Proposal”) in the above-

captioned proceeding. This proceeding has, for good reason, produced an already extensive

record, including 180 initial comments that collectively stretch over 2,500 pages. While the parties

may disagree on many aspects of how to achieve the principal goal laid out in Secretary Wright’s

letter—ensuring the “timely, orderly, and non-discriminatory” interconnection of large loads to

the transmission system—they overwhelmingly agree on the importance of that goal to our power

system, our economic growth, and our national security.

         The question now before the Commission is what conclusions to draw from that extensive

record and what actions it should take to ensure “timely, orderly, and non-discriminatory”

interconnection of large loads to the transmission system. Google continues to believe that the

challenge of interconnecting large loads to the transmission system is, at its core, an energy

infrastructure challenge.1 The reality is that our nation’s electric transmission infrastructure is


   1
       See Google Initial Comments at 2-5.
 failing to keep pace with the massive, concurrent demands being driven by electrification, the

resurgence of U.S. manufacturing, and the expansion of digital infrastructure. Inadequate electric

transmission infrastructure is becoming the principal limitation to interconnecting new large loads,

including data centers, and the needed generation capacity at the speed and scale necessary to

sustain our global economic competitiveness. As explained in Google’s initial comments, the

combination of aging infrastructure, decades of underinvestment, and fragmented, highly localized

planning practices have resulted in a transmission grid that is struggling to keep up with the

demands of this new growth, including from data centers.2 As a result, it takes too long to

interconnect new large loads and new generation, and the cost of doing so is too high. Lengthy

interconnection delays are directly driving up energy prices. When new supply remains locked in

a queue, it cannot meet rising demand in time, which puts upward pressure on all prices, including

for energy, capacity, and ancillary services. Resolving those bottlenecks by building the necessary

transmission infrastructure is one of the principal steps our nation can take to solve all of those

challenges.

         The record assembled in this docket so far corroborates that conclusion. A diverse set of

stakeholders have submitted a compelling evidentiary case that increasing transmission capacity

is essential to expediting the interconnection of large loads to the transmission system in order to

support national competitiveness, including winning the AI race.3 For example, the Data Center

“fundamentally an infrastructure challenge.”4 DCC points out that the grid as we know it today

was designed “to accommodate incremental changes in peak demand”—not to keep pace with the

unprecedented growth we are seeing today.5               Under existing reactive and siloed planning

individually and identify incremental transmission upgrades necessary to support those requests.”6

The result is “a hodgepodge development of the transmission system”7 and plans that “only

respond[] to present—or even past—reliability needs.”8 This piecemeal approach to transmission

infrastructure planning “will not deliver infrastructure on the timeline needed” to meet the present

needs of large load customers9 because “an approach which focuses solely on interconnecting large

loads to the electric grid will not fully support rapid data center and industrial load growth.”10

 Comments from grid operators,11 transmission owners,12 large load customers,13 and other

concerned parties14 echo similar exhortations to make transmission planning processes more

efficient and holistic, thereby reducing the barriers to building transmission infrastructure. The

record is clear: to get large load interconnection right, the Commission must consider the interplay

between transmission capacity and the interconnection of both large loads and the generators that

supply them.

         The way to address that foundational transmission issue is to adopt a holistic transmission

planning process that optimizes grid development by accounting for both generators and the large

loads planning to interconnect. Doing so will enable the United States to develop the most

efficient, cost-effective electric transmission backbone necessary to rapidly interconnect all loads,

including data centers, as well as the generation resources needed to provide them with reliable

 power. And time is of the essence: Absent a change of course, electric infrastructure appears to

be the one pillar of our economy and our global competitiveness where we are increasingly falling

behind,15 a result that would have devastating consequences for our economic growth and national

security. To avoid that result, the Commission should continue to support efforts to improve long-

term regional transmission planning processes,16 and reject measures that would complicate the

buildout of transmission facilities being developed as a result of those processes.17

         But even the best, most efficient transmission planning takes time, and the process of

planning, permitting, and building the necessary transmission infrastructure takes even longer.

That is time that we don’t have. To ensure our national competitiveness, the United States must

focus on expediting the development and interconnection of large loads, including data centers,

that maximize the use of existing transmission infrastructure and minimize strain on the grid. That

is the only way to build digital infrastructure at the “speed of national need”18 in the near-term

while we also develop the transmission infrastructure that will support our long-term economic

      ambitions. Accordingly, Google submits that this proceeding should also develop the rules and

     regulations that will facilitate and incentivize investments in both digital and energy infrastructure

     that maximize the utilization of the existing transmission system, allowing loads to start

     interconnecting now.

               As discussed further below, the record compiled to date in this proceeding identifies and

     explains multiple different ways that the Commission can achieve that goal. Google urges the

     Commission to act promptly to facilitate those pathways to efficient development of digital and

     energy infrastructure while at the same time not losing focus on the transmission development

     imperative that is necessary to achieve durable, lasting economic competitiveness of the United

     States.

I.      The Commission Should Focus on Maximizing Use of Existing Infrastructure and
        Minimizing Strain on the Grid

               The record in this proceeding provides strong support for several approaches to maximize

     the use of the existing transmission system and incentivize the investments in digital and energy

     infrastructure that do the same. Those include the co-location of load and generation behind the

     same point of interconnection,19 the integration of generators that are electrically proximate to new

proceeding, ensuring that any expedited processes are technology neutral and do not arbitrarily

flexibility.

   A. Expediting Co-Location to Minimize the Need for New Transmission Infrastructure

         There is broad agreement in the record that the co-location of loads and generation behind

the same point of interconnection is a promising vehicle to make the most out of the existing

infrastructure we have.23 As Constellation explains, “[o]ne of the primary attributes of co-location

configurations (all of them) is that they take advantage of existing infrastructure and

          The concerns that some commenters raise about co-location should not provide a reason to

forgo an efficient path to interconnecting significant sources of electricity demand with relatively

little dependence on the constrained transmission system. For instance, some parties argue that

load and generation studies cannot be combined because transmission providers need to model

each facility separately in case one trips.36 But even if the facilities must be modeled separately,

there is still significant value in improving the coordination of the studies. Doing so will align

project timelines, which can help reduce uncertainty and increase commercial readiness. Study

coordination will also help ensure that transmission providers select the most efficient transmission

network upgrades to accommodate the entire interconnection instead of less efficient, piecemeal

upgrades.

          There is also some debate in the record as to whether network upgrades and transmission

service should be designed based on gross load or net load.37 As CAISO explains, identifying

network upgrades to interconnect co-located facilities based on their requested injection and

Determining what network upgrades are required to accommodate the actual injection and

withdrawal rights requested and providing transmission service based on the actual use of the

transmission system will send the proper signals to encourage developers to pursue the most

efficient projects. Doing so will provide incentives to maximize the use of existing infrastructure

while minimizing strain on the grid and help get as much new demand online and powered up as

quickly as possible.

          Finally, some parties raise concerns about harming existing generator interconnection

processes that were recently revised to comply with Order No. 2023.40 Google agrees that the

Commission should do no harm to those processes, but facilitating co-located load and generation

need not necessarily occur within the existing generator interconnection cluster study process,

unless the transmission provider believes that doing so would be more efficient.41 In any case, the

Commission has a long history of authorizing regional variation, particularly in the RTO/ISO

         The concerns raised in the record about co-location are readily resolvable, and do not

outweigh its potential value in interconnecting new large loads in a manner that maximizes the use

of existing infrastructure and minimizes strain on the grid.            The Commission should act

expeditiously to facilitate a pathway to study and interconnect co-located facilities in a coordinated

and expedited manner. Nevertheless, any such pathway must be technology neutral. A

Commission-established fast track for loads using co-located generation to mitigate transmission

impacts should be paired with equivalent pathways to achieve the same end, including, for

example, using curtailment. Such pathways must be voluntary, incentive based, and limited only

to those loads that agree to meet the technical requirements of participating under the relevant

frameworks and include measures to ensure that they do, in fact, comply with those requirements.

The following sections provide a more detailed discussion on these additional pathways.

    B. Expediting the Interconnection of Electrically Proximate Generation and Load Can
      Help Grid Operators Get the Most out of Existing Infrastructure

         The record also provides strong support for facilitating the interconnection of generation

resources paired with new large loads, not just in traditional co-location configurations, but also

in electrically proximate pairs.43 DCC, for instance, contends that joint study of new, physically

proximate load and generation presents meaningful system benefits, which include reducing the

need for network upgrades, accelerating the timeline for bringing load and generation online,

improving resource adequacy, minimizing congestion and curtailment, and expanding siting

options.44 After all, “[i]t is obvious from basic engineering principles that generation located near

load requires less transmission infrastructure to serve that load than generation located distant from

load.”45 Google agrees with commenters that the Commission should establish pathways for

facilitating the expedited study and interconnection of electrically proximate pairs of generation

Separately, though relatedly, AEP urges the Commission to address generator interconnection queue
backlogs by enabling connect-and-manage interconnection. AEP Comments at 7-10. AEP urges the
Commission to look to the Electric Reliability Council of Texas’s (“ERCOT”) approach to “connect and

and manage approach, generators may interconnect to the transmission grid once they satisfy certain
technical criteria, even when network constraints remain or transmission upgrades are incomplete. Id.
According to AEP, “[a]ny grid bottlenecks caused by a new generator are managed by ERCOT through
market redispatch and curtailment, until they are later addressed through broader transmission planning
processes,” thereby decoupling interconnection from network expansion. Id.

          Notably, SPP’s recently filed High Impact Large Loads Generation Addition (“HILLGA”)

proposal—which has garnered support from a diverse set of stakeholders46—offers one example

of a framework for expediting the study and interconnection of new generation to serve electrically

proximate large loads. The HILLGA proposal allows for a generator which supports a proximate

High Impact Large Load (“HILL”) to opt into an interconnection process that allows for limited,

expedited interconnection and in which the generator is studied in 90 days.47              Generators

interconnecting via the HILLGA process receive Load Limited Resource Interconnection Service

(“LLRIS”), a limited and provisional form of interconnection service that allows the generator to

serve a nearby HILL, rather than traditional generator interconnection service (i.e., Network

Resource Interconnection Service (“NRIS”) or Energy Resource Interconnection Service

(“ERIS”)).48 After five years, LLRIS terminates and the generator must transition to NRIS or

ERIS.49

          The Commission can use some of the key concepts of the HILLGA proposal as a starting

point to create a regime for expediting the interconnection of new generation that is electrically

proximate to a new large load. Specifically, the Commission should ensure that any such regime:

   ● Provides an optional pathway (i.e., an incentive) and not a requirement that effectively
     blocks the interconnection of large loads that, for whatever reason, are not or cannot be
     paired with electrically proximate generation.

   ● Is time-limited and requires the generator to transition to full interconnection service on a
     definite timeline (e.g., the five-year limit in HILLS/HILLGA). This will help balance the
     competing interests of ensuring that new generators can interconnect quickly while also
     ensuring that, over the medium and long terms, we develop the necessary transmission
     infrastructure.

   ● Ensures that any expedited interconnection process is technology neutral. In particular, it
     must be open to storage resources, which can deploy more rapidly than any other grid
     resource and can manage the impact of large loads on the grid.50

   ● Create a study timeline and milestones that are both feasible and that facilitate the rapid
     interconnection of new generation resources. In this vein, the Commission should require
     that the system impact study be completed within 90 days and create a defined, time-limited
     negotiation window during which parties can negotiate an interconnection agreement.

   ● Ensure that generators using the expedited interconnection process are electrically
     proximate to the load they will serve during the period that they have limited
     interconnection service. On this point, Google agrees that what constitutes “electrical
     proximity” may vary by region and that the term should be defined at a sufficient level of
     generality “to allow consideration of capacity deliverable to the associated load such that
     it relieves, avoids, or minimizes congestion impacts.”51

   C. Creating a Framework to Facilitate and Incentivize the Voluntary Participation of

II.       Jurisdiction

                Even the most effective proposals for facilitating large load interconnection are beside the

      point of this proceeding if the Commission lacks the jurisdiction or authority to implement or

      approve them. With that in mind, Google provides the following perspective on the jurisdictional

      issues raised by Secretary Wright’s letter.

                Although Google agrees that the Commission has jurisdiction over the actual

      interconnection of large loads to the transmission system, it is important not to overstate the

      practical impact of that conclusion in the broader context of large load integration issues. Because

      states have exclusive jurisdiction over the rates, terms, and conditions of retail sales, every large

      load interconnection in the country will require active state involvement. The Commission

      affirmed that critical conclusion just weeks ago.78 And, as other commenters have recognized, the

      vast majority of the contents of recent large load tariffs enacted in many states around the country

      would not be affected, much less preempted, if the Commission were to conclude that the actual

      interconnection of large loads to the transmission falls within the Commission’s jurisdiction.79

         In addition, Google understands the potential reforms contemplated in the opening

comments to this proceeding to exist on a spectrum in terms of the jurisdictional questions that

a single point of interconnection raises the fewest jurisdictional questions, as it is already firmly

established that the generator’s interconnection agreement is within the Commission’s exclusive

jurisdiction, and the Commission does not lose jurisdiction by virtue of the fact that a retail sale

also takes place behind that point of interconnection.81 Similarly, because the Commission has

exclusive jurisdiction over the rates, terms, and conditions of transmission service, and the

 III.      Conclusion

              The Commission has before it a series of important and critical questions as well as a

       massive record on how it should answer those questions. Google submits that the Commission

       should focus on measures to expedite the development and interconnection of large loads,

       including data centers, that maximize the use of existing transmission infrastructure and minimize

       strain on the grid. Doing so now will do the most to protect all customers, promote our economic
